messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun Patel, a 29-year-old painter, came to treatment months after being mugged on his way home from a residential job. He had stayed late finishing trim in a vacant apartment building, carrying his backpack with brushes, cash from the day, and his phone. In the dim stretch between the train stop and his car, two men came up fast from behind a wall. What he remembers most clearly is the scrape of shoes, one man grabbing his shoulder, and the flash of a hand near his face as they demanded his bag. Other parts feel broken off or missing. He has told the story several times to his wife, but each time he gets stuck on fragments and cannot deliberately pull the whole sequence together. When he does get close to the memory, what hits him is a sharp guilt that he should have seen them earlier, should have fought harder, should not have been carrying cash.

In the weeks after, Arjun tried to return to work as if nothing had changed. But waking from nightmares left a residue that stayed in his body long after morning. On those days he would arrive at job sites already tense, shoulders tight, jaw set, moving room to room as if someone might step out from behind a doorway. Passing the block near the mugging, or even entering an unfamiliar apartment complex for work, could bring the scene into his mind all at once. A hallway with poor lighting, footsteps echoing on concrete, or the sight of an alcove would make his body surge into readiness before he could think. He began scanning stairwells, parking lots, and windows automatically, and if a client approached him suddenly with a question he could snap back irritably, embarrassed by how quickly he turned sharp or angry.

These moments also pulled at the memory itself. A location resembling the one where he was attacked could force up a sudden image of being grabbed, while leaving the rest inaccessible, as if the worst second of it was vivid and everything around it had dropped away. He found this especially unnerving after nightmares: he would wake with his heart pounding and a sense that something terrible had just happened, then spend the morning with bits of the robbery intruding into his mind without being able to place them in order. The more these fragments came uninvited, the more certain he became that the memory held something he had failed to do. That guilt on recall hardened into a broader conclusion that people were not safe and that he had been foolish to assume otherwise.

Since the robbery, Arjun had come to believe that people cannot be trusted and that relying on anyone leaves you exposed. He said this was the part his wife did not understand: she wanted to reassure him, but reassurance from other people no longer felt usable to him. He kept thinking that no one had been there when it mattered, and that in the end he was on his own. That belief has left him feeling cut off even at home. He sits apart, answers briefly, and watches the street from the apartment window at night. Being around strangers now carries an expectation of danger, and that expectation keeps his body braced; in crowded stores or on jobs in unfamiliar neighborhoods he scans faces, exits, and blind corners continuously, becoming irritable if anyone tells him he is overreacting.

Those same beliefs have made the world feel full of reminders. Because he is certain other people may take advantage of him, any physical location where he lacks control—a parking garage, an empty corridor, a stairwell in a building he has been hired to paint—starts to feel charged before anything happens. He notices himself listening for footsteps, and once he begins looking, ordinary cues quickly become triggers. A stranger lingering by an entrance, voices behind him, or waking from a nightmare after sleeping lightly will set off not only the bodily tension but also the sudden return of the memory fragments. In turn, those fragments deepen his conviction that something essential was missed and that he cannot rely on anyone to keep him safe.

What has frightened Arjun most is how self-sustaining it has become. The more incomplete the memory feels, the more he searches his surroundings for danger, as if vigilance could prevent another blind spot; the more he lives in that state, the more easily places and dream residue ignite the same images again. His wife has begun urging him not to take evening jobs because he comes home edgy and distant, and he has turned down work in larger apartment buildings because he cannot tolerate enclosed hallways without feeling his body gear up. He finally sought help after waking from a nightmare and nearly shouting at his wife when she touched his shoulder to calm him. He said he is afraid that if this continues he will lose both his work and his marriage, and he hopes, cautiously, that he might stop feeling as if danger is waiting in every corner.
